say: You've heard it a million times: lightning never strikes the same place twice. Cute saying. Totally wrong.
The Empire State Building gets hit by lightning about twenty three times a year, on average. It's basically a giant lightning magnet.
So how does lightning pick a target? Three things matter most: being tall, being pointy, and standing all alone.
And here's a surprise. Metal makes absolutely no difference to where lightning strikes. Tall, pointy and lonely is what wins.
Even one single flash cheats. After the first stroke, two or three more usually race down the exact same path.
That's why lightning seems to flicker. You're watching it hit the same spot again and again, all in a fraction of a second.
Scientists have even spotted flashes with more than a dozen strokes. One spot, zapped twelve times, in one flash.
And people? Park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven times between nineteen forty two and nineteen seventy seven. He survived every one.
One more twist. Lightning can strike ten to fifteen miles away from a storm, under blue sky. If you hear thunder, head inside.
So lightning strikes twice, and then some. Follow Simply Weird for more weird stuff like this.
